title: A Page of Talmud
bigQuestion: How can people all over the world open the same book to the same page on the same day?

story.title: Same Page, Two Cities
story.kicker: A grandmother in Skokie and a grandson in Denver open the same page on the same morning, and call each other about it.
paragraphs: It is early in Skokie, just north of Chicago. Miriam pours her tea and opens a thick book to the second page. The book is Berakhot, the first tractate of the Talmud. She reads the first line in Hebrew, then checks the English on her tablet. "From when do people say the evening Shema?" she reads. She writes the question on a sticky note.

A thousand miles away in Denver, her grandson Eli is eating cereal. He opens a website called Sefaria on his laptop and finds the same page: Berakhot 2a. He is eleven. The Hebrew is hard, so he reads the English. Today is the first day of a new cycle. Thousands of people, all over the world, are reading this exact page today.

At nine o'clock, Miriam's phone rings. "Grandma, why does it start with a question about bedtime?" Eli asks. Miriam laughs. "That is what I wanted to ask you," she says. They look at the page together, each on their own screen. In the middle is the Mishnah, and then the Gemara. Along the inside edge is a note from Rashi, who lived in France almost a thousand years ago.

"Rashi says the priests in this line are the ones who had to wait until dark," Miriam reads. "So the Mishnah is saying: night begins when the stars come out." Eli finds the same note in English. "So the first question in the whole Talmud is what time it is," he says. "Sort of," says Miriam. "It is when the day ends and the night begins."

They will do this again tomorrow, with page 2b. And the day after, with 3a. If they keep going, they will finish the whole Talmud in about seven and a half years. Eli will be eighteen. Miriam says she will be there for it. For now, they say goodbye. The page waits, the same page, in two cities.
story.think: Miriam and Eli read the same page but in different ways. What did each of them bring to it that the other did not?

lessons.title: One Leaf, Two Sides
lessons.mainIdea: A daf is one leaf with two sides, a and b, and every tractate starts at daf 2.
reading: Open a printed Talmud and you see a leaf, not a page. The rabbis call it a *daf*. Each daf has two sides. The front is called side a, and the back is side b. A side is called an *amud*, which means "column." So "Berakhot 2a" means tractate Berakhot, leaf 2, front side.

Why does every tractate start at daf 2? Because in the early printings the title page was daf 1. It had no Talmud on it. The first leaf with Gemara was leaf 2. Printers kept that habit for 500 years. Today every edition, in every country, still begins at 2a.

This is very useful. A teacher in Chicago can say "look at Berakhot 2a," and a student in Jerusalem, Buenos Aires or Denver will find the same words in the same spot. The page numbers are the same in every standard edition, so everyone can point to the same place.

words.d: one leaf of the Talmud, with two sides; the way pages of the Talmud are counted
one side of a daf; side a is the front and side b is the back

look.title: Reading a Citation
look.text: Here are three citations: Berakhot 2a. Shabbat 31a. Bava Metzia 59b. Each one has two parts. The first word is the name of the tractate, the book. The number is the leaf. The letter says which side: a for the front, b for the back. Berakhot means "blessings." Shabbat means "the Sabbath." Bava Metzia means "the middle gate."
look.prompt: For each citation, say the tractate, the leaf and the side. Which one is on the back of a leaf?

check.q: What does "Berakhot 2a" mean?
choices: The second book of the Mishnah
check.why: A citation names the tractate, the leaf (daf) and the side (a is the front, b is the back).

check.q: Why does every tractate begin at daf 2?

check.why: Early printers used leaf 1 as the title page, so the Gemara starts on leaf 2, and every edition kept that habit.

check.q: What is an amud?
check.why: An amud, meaning "column," is one side of a daf; there are two per leaf.

lessons.title: The Middle Column
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah and Gemara sit in the middle column of the page, with no vowels and no punctuation.
reading: Look at the middle of the page. That is the main text. It begins with a short piece of Mishnah, in Hebrew. The word "Mishnah" is often printed in big letters before it. Then comes the Gemara, in Aramaic, with the word "Gemara" in big letters before it. The two follow each other down the *column*.

The letters in the middle column are large and square. But there are no vowel marks, no periods and no question marks. Readers have to know where a sentence ends. Many words are cut short. An *abbreviation* is a shortened word. The Talmud is full of them, so a beginner needs help.

That is why people study out loud, and usually with a partner. One reads, the other checks. When the middle column is hard, the reader looks to the sides of the page, where the helpers wait. The first line of the whole Talmud, in Berakhot, is a question about when to say the evening Shema prayer.

words.d: a tall block of text on a page; the Mishnah and Gemara sit in the middle column
a shortened form of a word; the Talmud uses many of them

look.title: The First Line of the Talmud
look.text: The first Mishnah of tractate Berakhot asks: from what time may a person say the Shema in the evening? It answers: from the time the priests go in to eat their portion, and it gives other views about how late the Shema may be said. The Gemara then asks why the Mishnah begins with the evening and not the morning.
look.cite: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 and Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 2a, retold in plain words from the William Davidson Talmud (Sefaria, 2017)
look.prompt: The Mishnah gives a rule. The Gemara asks why the rule is written this way. What does that tell you about how the Gemara reads?

check.q: Where on the page are the Mishnah and the Gemara?
check.why: The Mishnah and Gemara run down the middle column; Rashi and Tosafot sit on the edges.

check.q: What is missing from the middle column that makes it hard to read?
check.why: The main text has no vowels, periods or question marks, and uses many abbreviations, so readers need help.

check.q: What is the first question in tractate Berakhot about?
choices: When to say the evening Shema
How to return a lost coat
check.why: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 asks from what time a person may say the Shema in the evening.

lessons.title: Words All Around
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi's explanation sits on the inside edge of the page and the Tosafot on the outside, so the page holds a conversation across centuries.
reading: Around the middle column run other blocks of text in smaller letters. On the inside edge, nearest the fold of the book, is the explanation by *Rashi*. He lived in France from 1040 to 1105. He explains hard words and fills in missing steps. Beginners read Rashi first when they get stuck.

On the outside edge are the *Tosafot*. The word means "additions." They were written by Rashi's grandsons and their students in the 1100s and 1200s. They ask hard questions. Often they say: but on another page the Talmud seems to say the opposite! Then they try to work it out.

The small letters on the sides are printed in a special font called Rashi script. Along the very edges are even smaller notes that point to other pages and to later law books. The page is like a table where a rabbi from the year 300, a teacher from 1100 and a printer from 1880 all sit and talk.

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105) of Troyes, France, whose explanation runs down the inside edge of the page
"additions": questions and answers by Rashi's grandsons and their students, printed on the outside edge

look.title: A Table Across Time
look.text: Picture a long table. At the head sits the Mishnah, from the year 200. Beside it sit the rabbis of the Gemara, from 200 to 500. Across from them sits Rashi, from the year 1100, explaining what they mean. Next to him sit his grandsons, asking him hard questions. At the far end sits a printer from 1880, setting every word in its place. You pull up a chair.
look.prompt: Which person at the table would you want to ask a question, and what would you ask?

check.q: Where is Rashi's explanation on the page?
choices: On the inside edge, near the fold
check.why: Rashi sits on the inside edge of the page; the Tosafot sit on the outside edge.

check.q: What does the word Tosafot mean?
check.why: Tosafot means "additions"; they add questions and answers to the page.

check.q: Who wrote the Tosafot?
check.why: The Tosafot were written in France and Germany in the 1100s and 1200s by Rashi's grandsons and their students.

lessons.title: Rashi, the Teacher From Troyes
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi wrote a clear, step-by-step commentary on almost the whole Babylonian Talmud, and readers have leaned on it ever since.
reading: Rashi is a short name made from the first letters of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki. He was born in 1040 in *Troyes*, a town in northern France, and died there in 1105. As a young man he studied in schools along the Rhine river in Germany. Then he came home and taught.

Rashi wrote a *commentary*, an explanation that follows a text line by line. He did it for the Torah and for almost all of the Babylonian Talmud. His style is plain. He tells you what a word means. He tells you who is speaking. He fills in a missing step so the argument makes sense.

Jewish readers of every kind, Orthodox, Conservative and Reform, still study with Rashi. So do university scholars. His Torah commentary was one of the first Hebrew books ever printed, in 1475. When printers made the Talmud page, they gave Rashi the inside edge, the place closest to the text.

words.d: a town in northern France where Rashi was born, taught and died
an explanation that follows a text line by line

look.title: Rashi Explains a Hard Word
look.text: The first Mishnah says the evening Shema may be said from the time the priests go in to eat their portion. Which priests? Rashi explains: priests who had become impure, then washed, and had to wait until the stars came out before they could eat. So, Rashi says, the Mishnah means the Shema may be said from nightfall.
look.cite: Rashi on Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 2a, retold in plain words from the William Davidson Talmud (Sefaria, 2017)
look.prompt: The Mishnah did not say "nightfall." How did Rashi get there? What did he add?

check.q: Where did Rashi live?
check.why: Rashi was born, taught and died in Troyes, in northern France (1040–1105).

check.q: What is a commentary?
choices: An explanation that follows a text line by line
check.why: A commentary explains a text step by step; Rashi wrote one on the Torah and on the Talmud.

check.q: What does Rashi usually do in his notes?
choices: Argues that the Gemara is wrong
Tells stories about his own life
Explains hard words and fills in missing steps
check.why: Rashi's style is plain: he says what a word means, who is speaking and what step is missing.

lessons.title: Tosafot, the Questioners
lessons.mainIdea: The Tosafot compare one page of Talmud with another and ask why they seem to disagree.
reading: Rashi had daughters, and their sons became great teachers. One grandson was called *Rabbeinu Tam*. Another was the Rashbam. They and their students, in France and Germany in the 1100s and 1200s, wrote the Tosafot. They loved Rashi. They also argued with him.

The Tosafot ask a special kind of question. They remember the whole Talmud at once. So they say: here the Gemara says one thing, but on a page in another tractate it says the opposite. That is a *contradiction*. Then they find a difference between the two cases that explains both.

Reading the Tosafot is like watching a chess player think many moves ahead. Their notes are harder than Rashi's, so students usually learn Rashi first. But the Tosafot show what Talmud study became: not only reading a page, but holding the whole book in your head and asking it to agree with itself.

words.d: Rashi's grandson (about 1100–1171), a leading writer of the Tosafot
two statements that seem to say opposite things; the Tosafot look for these and try to explain them

look.title: A Tosafot-Style Question at School
look.text: The school rule book says: no running in the halls. The gym rule book says: run three laps at the start of class. A Tosafot-style reader asks: do the rules contradict each other? Then answers: no, the hall rule is about safety in a crowded space, and the gym rule is about exercise in an open one. Each rule fits its own place.
look.prompt: Find two rules at school or at home that seem to disagree. Can you find the difference between the cases that makes both rules make sense?

check.q: Who was Rabbeinu Tam?
choices: Rashi's grandson and a writer of the Tosafot
The head of the academy at Sura
check.why: Rabbeinu Tam, a grandson of Rashi, was one of the leading writers of the Tosafot in the 1100s.

check.q: What kind of question do the Tosafot ask most?
choices: Why does this page seem to disagree with another page?
check.why: The Tosafot compare pages across the whole Talmud and try to explain apparent contradictions.

check.q: Why do students usually learn Rashi before the Tosafot?
choices: Rashi's notes are plainer and the Tosafot are harder
The Tosafot are not printed on the page
check.why: Rashi explains words and steps simply; the Tosafot expect a reader to hold many pages in mind at once.

lessons.title: Printers Who Fixed the Page
lessons.mainIdea: A printer in Venice set the page's shape in the 1520s, and the Vilna printing of the 1880s made it the page everyone uses.
reading: For a thousand years the Talmud was copied by hand. Each copy looked different. Then came the *printing press*. In Venice, Italy, between 1520 and 1523, a printer named Daniel Bomberg printed the whole Babylonian Talmud. Bomberg was a Christian. His Jewish editors helped him plan the page.

Bomberg's page put the Mishnah and Gemara in the middle, Rashi on the inside and the Tosafot on the outside. He numbered the leaves. Printers who came after him copied his page numbers, so that Berakhot 2a stayed Berakhot 2a everywhere.

The most famous printing came from *Vilna*, today the city of Vilnius in Lithuania. The Romm family press printed it between 1880 and 1886. The press was run by a widow, Deborah Romm, with her brothers-in-law. The Vilna edition added more notes around the edges. It became the standard page, copied by nearly every edition since.

words.d: a machine that presses inked type onto paper, so many copies of a book look exactly the same
today's Vilnius, Lithuania, where the Romm press printed the standard edition of the Talmud in 1880–1886

lessons.title: Daf Yomi Begins
lessons.mainIdea: Daf Yomi, started in 1923, has people everywhere read one daf a day and finish the whole Talmud in about seven and a half years.
reading: In 1923 a young rabbi from Poland, Meir Shapiro of Lublin, stood up at a big meeting of Jewish leaders in Vienna. He had an idea. What if Jews everywhere read the same daf on the same day? One page a day, every day, until the whole Babylonian Talmud was done. He called it *Daf Yomi*, "the daily page."

The plan was simple. Day one is Berakhot 2a. Day two is Berakhot 2b. The Bavli has 2,711 leaves, so one *cycle* takes 2,711 days, about seven years and five months. When the last page is read, the next day starts again at Berakhot 2a.

Rabbi Shapiro said a traveler could get off a train in any city, walk into a study hall and find people on the same page. It worked. The first cycle began in September 1923. Since then the cycle has run without a break, through wars and hard years, with people joining and leaving along the way.

words.d: "the daily page": a plan begun in 1923 in which people everywhere read the same daf of Talmud each day
one full trip through all 2,711 leaves of the Babylonian Talmud, about seven and a half years

lessons.title: A Stadium Full of Readers
lessons.mainIdea: When a cycle ends, readers gather for a siyum, and in 2020 tens of thousands filled a stadium to celebrate.
reading: Finishing a book of Talmud is a happy day. Jewish tradition marks it with a *siyum*, a celebration of finishing. People read the last lines, say a special prayer, and share a meal. When a whole Daf Yomi cycle ends, the celebration is called the Siyum HaShas, the finishing of the whole Talmud.

On January 1, 2020, the thirteenth cycle ended. About 90,000 people filled MetLife Stadium in New Jersey for a Siyum HaShas. Days later, thousands of women gathered in Jerusalem for a siyum of their own, since more women now study the daily page too. Groups met in many cities, including Chicago.

The next cycle began on January 5, 2020, with Berakhot 2a. Since then the readers have moved together through tractate after tractate. Some study in a hall with a teacher. Some listen to a podcast on the train. Some read with a grandchild on the phone. The page is the same for all of them.

words.d: a celebration of finishing a book of Talmud, with the last lines read aloud, a prayer and a meal
the celebration held when a whole Daf Yomi cycle of the Talmud is finished

look.title: Ninety Thousand Readers
look.text: Picture a football stadium on a cold January night. Every seat is full. But no one is watching a game. On the big screens is the last page of the last tractate. A voice reads the final lines. Then a prayer. Then a song, and people in the stands dancing in their coats. Some of them have read a page a day for seven and a half years.
look.prompt: Why might people want to celebrate finishing a book together, in a crowd, instead of quietly at home?

lessons.title: Finding Berakhot Page 2
lessons.mainIdea: Anyone can find Berakhot 2a, in a book or online, and read it best with a partner.
reading: Here is how to find the first page. The Mishnah has six orders. The first order is *Zera'im*, "Seeds," about farming and blessings. Its first tractate is Berakhot, "Blessings." Find the volume marked Berakhot. Open it past the title page to daf 2. Side a is on your left when the book is open the Hebrew way.

You can also find it online. A free website called Sefaria shows the Hebrew and Aramaic beside an English translation. It lets you click on Rashi and the Tosafot. Type "Berakhot 2a" and the page appears. Many people in Chicago and around the world read the daily page this way.

The best way to read is with a *chavruta*, a study partner. One reads a line. The other asks what it means. When you are stuck, you look at Rashi together. The Talmud says students learn from their teachers, more from their friends, and most from the questions of their own students.

words.d: "Seeds," the first of the six orders of the Mishnah; Berakhot is its first tractate
a study partner; the word means "friendship"

look.title: Learning From Everyone
look.text: In tractate Ta'anit, Rabbi Chanina says that he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and most of all from his students. On the same page another teacher compares two scholars studying together to iron sharpening iron: each one makes the other sharper.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 7a, retold in plain words from the William Davidson Talmud (Sefaria, 2017)
look.prompt: Why might a teacher learn the most from students? What do students do that teachers do not?

check.q: Which order of the Mishnah is Berakhot in?
